a: twenty-fifth year since we were taken into exile
t: The date: spring or autumn of 573 BC
p: The last dated vision in the book, twenty-five years after Jehoiachin's exile and fourteen years after Jerusalem fell.
b: Ezekiel counts from King Jehoiachin's deportation in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12-16), and he also counts from the fall of the city, which this site dates to 586 BC. Both counts land in 573/572 BC, which is why it is usually given as 573. The phrase "the start of the year" (Hebrew rosh hashanah, "head of the year") is uncertain: if the year began in spring, the tenth of the month is the tenth of Nisan (about April); if it began in autumn, it is the tenth of Tishri. Some scholars date the fall of Jerusalem to 587 BC, which shifts these numbers by a year. This is the last of Ezekiel's dated visions; the latest dated oracle in the book is 29:17 (571 BC). The vision runs to the end of the book (chapters 40-48).

a: the tenth day of the month
t: The tenth of the month: Jubilee or Day of Atonement?
p: The rabbis read the date as the tenth of Tishri, the Day of Atonement, in a Jubilee year.
b: The Talmud reads "the start of the year, the tenth day of the month" as the tenth of Tishri, and so as the Day of Atonement, and counts the year as a Jubilee year, when the horn was blown and slaves went free (Leviticus 25:9-10). This reading appears in the Babylonian Talmud (Rosh Hashanah 8b; Arakhin 12a). It fits a vision of a purified Temple. The other reading is spring: the tenth of Nisan, the day Israel chose the Passover lamb (Exodus 12:3), the day Israel crossed the Jordan (Joshua 4:19). The text itself does not choose. Both readings tie the vision to a day of beginning and release.

a: the hand of the LORD came on me
t: "The hand of the LORD": the prophet seized
p: Ezekiel's phrase for the moment a vision takes hold of him, from his first vision to his last.
b: "The hand of the LORD" is Ezekiel's own phrase for the force that takes hold of him before a vision or a sign act (1:3; 3:14, 22; 8:1; 33:22; 37:1). It is used here for the last time, with the same words as in 1:3. The last vision opens as the first did, in the place where the prophet is: in Babylon, with his body in the exile and his sight in the land of Israel.

t: Carried to the land in a vision, not in the body
p: As in 8:3, the trip is a vision. Ezekiel does not leave Babylon.
b: The same words, "visions of God", open Ezekiel's first vision (1:1) and his tour of the old Temple (8:3). The tour of the new Temple is a vision too. The prophet is not described as walking in Jerusalem; he is "brought" and "set down", as in 8:3 and 11:1. A first reader in Babylon would know that the land was seventy-odd miles of desert away and that the Temple was a ruin; the vision shows the place as it will be, not as it is.

t: The very high mountain
p: Mount Zion is only a modest hill. In the vision it becomes the highest place in the world.
b: The real hill of the Temple stands about 2,400 feet above sea level, not a "very high mountain". The vision lifts it to match what other prophets said of the LORD's mountain (Isaiah 2:2; Micah 4:1; compare Psalm 48:1-2). The same book calls Eden "the holy mountain of God" (28:14), and Sinai was a mountain too, so a high mountain tells the reader that heaven and earth meet here. Revelation 21:10 borrows the picture: an angel carries John to a great, high mountain to see the holy city. The book never names the mountain Zion; it is simply the place the LORD has chosen.
r: Isaiah 2:2-3; Micah 4:1; Psalm 48:1-2; Ezekiel 28:14; Ezekiel 20:40; Revelation 21:10

a: what looked like the buildings of a city
t: A city to the south of the Temple
p: The Temple stands north of the city, which is where the Temple stood in real Jerusalem too.
b: The city lies to the south of the Temple area in the vision. That matches the real map: Solomon built the Temple north of the old City of David. But the city of the vision is not Jerusalem as it was; it is "something like" a city (compare the careful "like" in chapter 1), and its measurements come only at the end of the book, as a square of 4,500 cubits on each side (48:15-17), with the name "The LORD Is There" (48:35). The Greek has "opposite" where the Hebrew has "south" (see the variant).

a: a man whose appearance was like bronze
t: The man with the cord and the reed
p: A shining guide, like the figure of fire in 8:2, measures the whole Temple with a linen cord and a reed.
b: The guide is a heavenly being, not named. His look is "like bronze" (compare Daniel 10:5-6, where a man in linen has arms and legs that gleam like polished bronze). He stays at the prophet's side through chapters 40-48 and speaks to him (40:4; 43:6-7; 44:5; 47:3-6). A man with a measuring line also appears in Zechariah 1:16 and 2:1-5, where he measures Jerusalem, and an angel with a measuring rod appears in Revelation 11:1 and 21:15-17. The linen cord was used for long measures and the reed for short ones (compare 47:3-5).

a: Tell the house of Israel everything you are about to see
t: The prophet must report what he sees
p: The tour has one purpose: the exiles must hear it. The command returns in 43:10-11.
b: Ezekiel is not given the plan for himself. As a watchman (3:16-21) he must pass it on, "everything you are about to see", and the purpose is spelled out in 43:10-11: when the people are ashamed of what they have done, he is to show them the Temple's plan, so that they keep its "design" and "rules". Compare the scroll Ezekiel ate in 2:8-3:4 and the command to John in Revelation 1:11, 19. The words "son of man" are explained at 2:1.

t: The long cubit and the measuring reed
p: Every length in these chapters is counted in a cubit that is about a hand's width longer than the ordinary one.
b: A common cubit was the length from elbow to fingertip, about 18 inches (45 cm), divided into six handbreadths. Here each cubit is "a cubit and a handbreadth", seven handbreadths, which is about 20.5 inches or 52 cm by the usual estimate. The reed is six of these long cubits, about 10 feet or 3.1 meters. Compare 43:13, which repeats the definition for the altar. 2 Chronicles 3:3 also speaks of a particular measure of cubits for Solomon's Temple. The Greek has the same definition. All the figures in the glosses below use the 52 cm cubit.

a: the width of the structure, one reed, and its height, one reed
t: A wall to keep the holy apart
p: A wall about 10 feet thick and 10 feet high is a boundary, not a defense.
b: The Hebrew says "the width of the structure" (rochav habbinyan) and its "height"; the Plain reads the width as the wall's thickness. The outer wall (40:5) is as thick as it is high, about 10 feet (3 m), and it runs all around the complex. It has no towers or battlements, and the gates in it (40:6-16, 20-27) are large gate-houses. The reason is given in 42:20: the wall is there "to separate the holy from the ordinary". Ezekiel had seen the opposite in chapter 8: a Temple where the unclean and the holy stood side by side. See also the contrast at 43:8, where the old Temple shared its wall with the king's house.

a: a gate whose front faced east
t: Gates of this shape from Solomon's day
p: The gate with three chambers on each side matches city gates that archaeologists have dug up in Israel.
b: The east gate has an outer porch, three chambers on each side of a central passage, and an inner porch. This is the layout of the six-chambered gates found by archaeologists at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer in layers dated to the 10th century BC (the date, and whether it is Solomon's, is debated). Yigael Yadin, who dug at Hazor, drew the likeness to Ezekiel's gates (in his book Hazor, 1975). Ezekiel's gates are bigger and they are copied three times: east, north and south, then again for the inner court. This is the gate by which the glory comes back in 43:1-4 and which is then shut in 44:1-3.

t: The gate chambers
p: The "chambers" are small rooms in the walls of the gate where guards or gate officers stood.
b: The Hebrew ta' is a small room, probably a guard post, built into the gate. The Plain uses "chamber" for ta' every time. Other rooms in this vision are lishkah, "room" (40:17; 42:1), and tsela', "side room" (41:5). The text counts 3 + 3 chambers per gate, each six cubits square (40:7, 12), with five cubits of wall between them. In 40:7-9 the Hebrew says the porch is "from the house" (mehabbayit); the Plain renders it "on the side toward the house" each time. The Greek has "inside".

a: He made pillars of sixty cubits
t: A garbled verse about the pillars
p: The numbers do not fit, and the Greek reads "twenty". The Plain follows the Hebrew and flags the problem.
b: This verse is one of the hardest in the chapter. "Sixty cubits" does not fit a gate that is 25 cubits wide (40:13) and 50 long (40:15), and "He made" is an odd verb for measuring. The word for "pillar" ('ayil) is also read as "porch" ('ulam), which would fit the next clause. The Greek has "twenty cubits". The Plain follows the Masoretic Text; no scroll preserves the verse, and the Greek may be a reading of a damaged text, or a guess at one.

t: Closed windows
p: A similar phrase appears in the description of Solomon's Temple, and its meaning is unclear.
b: The Hebrew challonim 'atumim means literally "closed windows". It may mean windows with recessed frames, windows fitted with lattice, or windows narrowing toward the outside so that no one could look in. A similar phrase is used for Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 6:4 has challonei shequfim 'atumim, windows of a different kind in the same description), and Ezekiel's phrase recurs in 41:16, 26. The windows face inward, toward the gate passage; what they were for is not stated.

t: Palm trees on the pillars
p: Palms on the gate pillars begin a pattern that continues inside the house.
b: Palm trees decorate the gate pillars (40:16, 22, 26, 31, 34, 37) and the walls inside the house (41:18-20, 25-26). Solomon's Temple had palm carvings too (1 Kings 6:29, 32, 35). A palm is a tree of life and of victory (Psalm 92:12), and with the cherubim of 41:18-20 it makes a garden, as in Eden (Genesis 2-3; compare Ezekiel 28:13-14; 31:8-9). Readers who had known the old Temple would have remembered its carved palms. See 41:18.

t: Rinsing the burnt offering
p: The rule is Leviticus 1:9, 13: the inner parts and legs of the animal are washed before they are burned.
b: A burnt offering was cut up and its inner parts and legs washed in water before they were burned on the altar (Leviticus 1:9, 13). In Solomon's Temple the washing was done in basins (2 Chronicles 4:6). Ezekiel puts this room at the inner gates, where the animals are killed; this fits the north-side rule of Leviticus 1:11 for slaughter. Here the room is a small thing, but it shows that Ezekiel's Temple works by the old law, with details adjusted.

a: the burnt offering, the sin offering and the guilt offering
t: The three kinds of offering slaughtered here
p: The animals for three of the main sacrifices are killed on these eight tables, as the law of Moses requires.
b: The north side is the place where the burnt offering is killed (Leviticus 1:11), and the sin offering is killed in the place where the burnt offering is slaughtered (Leviticus 4:24), as is the guilt offering (Leviticus 7:2). Ezekiel puts all three in the gate porches of the inner court, at the north side (40:40-41), and the sacrifice of a peace offering is not named here. The Greek mentions only the sin offering and the offering for sins of ignorance (see the variant).

t: Hooks, or ledges, or forks
p: The word is found nowhere else, and its meaning is guessed.
b: The Hebrew shefattayim occurs here and in Psalm 68:13 (where it means something like "sheepfolds" or "saddlebags"). Here it is read three ways: hooks (to hang the carcasses), ledges (a raised edge to keep the blood in) or two-pronged forks (for handling the meat). The Plain says "hooks" because the text says they were "fixed" in the wall, but the Greek has a carved ledge. Whatever it was, it was a handbreadth, 7 or 8 inches.

t: Rooms for singers: in the Hebrew only
p: Levite singers served in Solomon's Temple and the Second Temple, but only the Hebrew of this verse puts them in Ezekiel's Temple.
b: David set Levites over the music of the house of the LORD (1 Chronicles 6:31-32; 25:1-7), and singers were counted among the returning exiles (Ezra 2:41). The Hebrew calls these two rooms "rooms for singers" (lishkot sharim), the only mention of singers in Ezekiel's Temple. The Greek has "two rooms" and no word for singers (see the variant), and 40:45-46 give the same two rooms to the priests, so the singers belong to the Hebrew text of this verse alone. Whether the word was added in Hebrew or dropped in Greek cannot be settled from the evidence read here. The two texts also differ on where the second room stood (the east gate in the Hebrew, the south gate in the Greek). Ezekiel 44:10-14 demotes the Levites who went astray to duties at the gates and the house, and singers are not mentioned again in these chapters.

t: The sons of Zadok, first mention
p: Only Zadok's family are allowed to come near the altar. The chapter-44 rules are built on this verse.
b: Zadok was David's priest and Solomon's (2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Kings 1:8, 32-39; 2:35). The Plain says "the sons of Zadok" (Hebrew benei tsadoq) each time, and here they are the priests who "keep watch over the altar" and "come near to the LORD", from among the sons of Levi. Verse 45 gives the other room to "the priests who keep watch over the house". Chapter 44 explains the split: the Levites who went astray with the idols lose the right to serve at the altar, and the Zadokites keep it (44:10-16). See also 43:19, and the topic on Zadok.

t: Two columns at the porch
p: Free-standing columns at the porch recall Jachin and Boaz in front of Solomon's Temple.
b: Solomon's Temple had two bronze columns at its porch, named Jachin and Boaz (1 Kings 7:15-22; 2 Chronicles 3:15-17). Ezekiel mentions columns by the porch pillars, one on each side, but does not give their names, size or material. Whether he means the same pair, standing outside the porch as in Kings, or posts beside the doorframe, is not clear from the Hebrew. Solomon's porch was twenty cubits across and ten deep (1 Kings 6:3); Ezekiel's is twenty across and eleven deep in the Hebrew (twelve in the Greek), counted in the long cubit.

t: The great hall (hekhal)
p: The Hebrew word for the large main room of a temple is a loan from Mesopotamia, where it meant a palace.
b: The Hebrew hekhal is the large room in front of the innermost room (the "main hall" or "nave"). It comes from Akkadian ekallu, "palace", which in turn comes from Sumerian e-gal, "big house". It is the word of 1 Kings 6:3, 5, 17, which this site's Kings renders "great hall", and it is the same word that later means "temple" in general. In Ezekiel's Temple the great hall is 40 cubits long and 20 wide (41:2), the same number of cubits as Solomon's (1 Kings 6:2, 17), though Ezekiel's cubit is the long one (see 40:5).

t: "Tent" in the Hebrew, "porch" in the Greek
p: The Hebrew word is 'ohel, "tent". Many readers think a scribe wrote it for 'ulam, "porch".
b: The Masoretic Text reads 'ohel, "tent", a word that can stand for the Tabernacle (Exodus 26:36) and can be used poetically of a house. But the Greek reads "porch" (ailam) here and gives the porch's measurements, and many commentators take 'ohel as a slip for 'ulam (the two words share two letters). The Plain follows the Hebrew as it stands. See the variant at this verse.

t: Only the guide goes into the inner room
p: The prophet is not led into the innermost room. He waits at the door while his guide goes in alone.
b: The verb changes from "he brought me" to "he went" (41:3). The man goes into the innermost room by himself, and Ezekiel, a priest's son, stays outside. In Leviticus 16 only the high priest enters the most holy place, and only once a year. The text stays quiet about what the room holds: it does not mention the ark, the mercy seat or the cherubim of Solomon's Temple (1 Kings 8:6-7). The vision gives the room its measurements and nothing more (41:4). Qumran's 4QEzek-a (4Q73) has the measures of this verse and reads as the Masoretic Text does; the editors restore its first words and the word "cubits" at the end. The Greek has the guide go into "the inner court" and makes seven cubits the thickness of each side of the doorway (see the variant).

t: "The most holy place", and what is missing from it
p: The room is a 20-cubit cube. Nothing in it is described, not even the ark that stood in Solomon's.
b: The innermost room is 20 cubits by 20 (41:4), the same number of cubits as Solomon's (1 Kings 6:20), in the long cubit. The Hebrew calls it qodesh haqqodashim, "holy of holies", which is the site's "most holy place". In Solomon's Temple the ark and two large cherubim stood there; Ezekiel's description never mentions an ark. Jeremiah 3:16 had said that in the days of renewal people would no longer speak of the ark of the covenant or remember it. In Ezekiel the place of the LORD's throne is given by his own glory (43:7). The Plain uses "most holy" for qodesh qodashim in every use, including 42:13, 43:12. The Greek of 41:4 has forty cubits for the length (see the variant); 4Q73 has twenty, like the Masoretic Text.

t: "Three and thirty times"
p: The Hebrew count may mean thirty-three, or three stories of thirty. The Qumran copy has the same words.
b: The Hebrew is shalosh u-sheloshim pe'amim, "three and thirty times", and the Plain gives it as "thirty-three times". Readers differ on what is counted. One reading takes it as thirty-three rooms in all; another takes "three" and "thirty" separately, as three stories with thirty side rooms on each (ninety in all), which is what a comma form ("three, thirty times") would say. 4QEzek-a (4Q73) preserves these words without restoration and reads "three and thirty times" like the Masoretic Text. The Greek has "thirty, three times, twice" (triakonta tris dis), which does not make the count clearer. As in Solomon's Temple, the side rooms rest on supports that do not cut into the wall of the house (1 Kings 6:6).

a: The side rooms grew wider as they went up
t: The widening side rooms
p: In Solomon's Temple the side rooms also grew wider on each story.
b: In 1 Kings 6:6 the lowest side rooms were five cubits wide, the middle six and the third seven, because the temple wall was made thinner as it rose. Ezekiel's text says the same thing about the shape: the building "was wider higher up", and one climbed from the lowest level to the highest by the middle. The Hebrew is hard, and the Greek is no clearer.

t: "To the joint"
p: An unusual Hebrew word gives the foundation height. It may mean the corner joint of the wall.
b: The Hebrew 'atsilah is a rare word, perhaps related to the word for "nobles" in Exodus 24:11. Here it is read as "to the joint" (the point where the wall meets the next course or the platform) or "to the armpit", that is, a corner. A foundation height of six cubits, a full reed, is clear; what it measures to is not. The Greek has no word for it.

t: The "separate area" behind the house
p: A cut-off yard of ground on the west side of the house, with a building at its far end.
b: The Hebrew gizrah is from the root gazar, "to cut off", and means a cut-off or reserved strip. It runs around the house (41:12-15; 42:1, 10, 13). The Greek renders it "the remainder" and "the dividing part" in different places. The "building" (binyan) on the west is 70 cubits wide and 90 long (41:12), and its purpose is not stated. "West" is "toward the sea", the Mediterranean, in the Hebrew. See 46:19-24 for kitchens that may be in this part of the court.

t: A broken end to 41:15-17
p: These verses are among the book's hardest. The Plain follows the Hebrew and does not tidy it.
b: Verses 15b-17 are one long run of nouns in Hebrew: the great hall, the porches, the thresholds, the windows, the galleries. The word "galleries" ('attiqim) occurs only in 41:15-16 and 42:3, 5, and the Masoretes noted a spelling difference in 41:15. "By measure" is one Hebrew word, middot, "measures", which some take with the next verse as part of the carving. The Greek has no word for it and runs straight on to the carvings of 41:18.

a: Cherubim and palm trees were made
t: Cherubim and palm trees: Eden in the Temple
p: The walls show a garden: winged guardians between palm trees. It recalls Eden and Solomon's Temple.
b: Solomon's Temple walls were carved with cherubim, palm trees and open flowers (1 Kings 6:29). A cherub guarded the way to the tree of life in Eden (Genesis 3:24), and Ezekiel himself sets cherubim in the garden of Eden (28:13-14, 16). Beale and Levenson, among others, read the carved walls as a picture of the Temple as a small Eden, a place where the LORD and humans meet again. The cherubim here are carvings, not the living creatures of chapters 1 and 10.

t: Two faces, not four
p: The carved cherubim have a human face and a lion's face, not the four faces of chapter 1.
b: In Ezekiel's first vision each living creature has four faces: a human, a lion, an ox and an eagle (1:10). In 10:14 the ox face is called "the face of a cherub", and the creatures are named cherubim (10:15, 20). The carved cherubim of the Temple have only two faces, a human and a young lion (41:19). They face a palm tree on each side, so the human looks one way and the lion the other. The carvings are not the throne-bearers of chapter 1; they are guardians of a garden.

a: This is the table that is before the LORD.
t: An altar that is also a table
p: Three cubits high and made of wood, it is called both altar and table. Which furniture does this mean?
b: The Hebrew calls the object an "altar" (mizbeach) and then, in the guide's words, "the table that is before the LORD". The Tabernacle's table of the bread of the presence was wood overlaid with gold (Exodus 25:23-30), and its incense altar was also of wood overlaid with gold (Exodus 30:1-3). Ezekiel's piece is 3 cubits high, higher than either. Commentators read it as the table of the bread, the incense altar, or one object that does both jobs. The vision mentions no lampstand. The Greek joins this with the unfinished end of 41:21 (see the variants).

t: Folding doors, like Solomon's
p: The doors, with leaves hinged to fold, match what 1 Kings 6:34 says of the doors of the great hall.
b: Solomon made two folding doors of cypress for the great hall, each in two panels that turned on pivots (1 Kings 6:34). The words are close. The great hall and the inner room each have a doorway with two doors, and each door has two leaves (41:23-24). Both the doors of the great hall and of the inner room are carved with cherubim and palm trees (41:25), as in 1 Kings 6:32, 35.

t: A wooden canopy, not a threshold
p: The Hebrew 'av is a rare word. It is read as a canopy, an overhang, a beam or thick planks.
b: The word occurs here, in 41:26 (in the plural) and in 1 Kings 7:6, where it seems to be a porch roof or canopy; it is also read as an overhang, a beam or thick planks. The Plain says "a wooden canopy" here and "the canopies" in 41:26. It keeps "threshold" for a different word, sippim (41:16). The Greek reads "choice wood" here. It was in front of the porch, outside. The meaning is not settled.

t: The priests' rooms in the other Temples
p: Rooms for the priests stood around Solomon's Temple and the Second Temple.
b: Solomon's Temple had rooms (1 Chronicles 28:12; Jeremiah 35:2, 4; 36:10), including the room of Gemariah son of Shaphan, from which Baruch read Jeremiah's scroll (Jeremiah 36:10). The returned exiles stored the tithe in rooms in the Second Temple, and Tobiah the Ammonite was given one of them (Nehemiah 13:4-9). Ezekiel's two blocks of rooms, north and south of the great hall, are for the priests, who eat the most holy offerings there and change their clothes (42:13-14). The description is the hardest of the chapter.

a: gallery faced gallery on three levels
t: Galleries and ledges in 42:3-6
p: The Hebrew is one of the worst-preserved passages in the book; the Greek gives a much shorter text.
b: The Hebrew of 42:3-12 is full of rare words, among them 'attiqim, "galleries". The Plain follows the Hebrew: three levels of rooms, each set back from the one below, since the upper rooms "had no columns" to hold more weight (42:6). The Greek is shorter and speaks of rooms in rows, facing each other, with triple porches. Scholars differ on a clear plan, and the Plain does not try to draw one.

a: will eat the most holy things
t: Where the priests eat their share
p: The law of Moses says the priests eat certain offerings in a holy place. Ezekiel gives the place.
b: The priests' share of the grain offering, sin offering and guilt offering is "most holy" and must be eaten in a holy place, by male priests only (Leviticus 6:16-18, 26, 29; 7:6; 10:12-13). The Torah's "holy place" is the court of the Tabernacle. Ezekiel's text says where it is in the Temple: the rooms of 42:1-12. 44:28-31 gives the priests' portions again.

a: lay down the clothes they serve in
t: Holiness that spreads
p: The garments of service are holy and must be left before the priests mix with the people.
b: In the Torah the holy garments of the high priest are left in the holy place when he comes out on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:23-24). Ezekiel makes it a rule for all priests: they put on other clothes before going out among the people, so that they do not pass holiness on to them (44:19; 46:20). Ezekiel gives no further reason, and commentators differ on what the danger is (compare Exodus 29:37; 30:29).

a: He measured the east side with the measuring reed
t: Five hundred reeds, or five hundred cubits?
p: The text counts in reeds, which would make a square about 1 mile on each side, a huge space. Other readings say cubits.
b: See the variants. Five hundred reeds is 3,000 cubits, about 1 mile (1.6 km), larger than the old city of Jerusalem. Five hundred cubits is about 850 feet (260 m), a size that fits the surrounding vision. 42:20 gives the same numbers without a unit in the Hebrew, and 45:2 also gives 500 by 500 without one (only the surrounding strip of fifty is in cubits). The case for cubits therefore rests on context and on a few witnesses: the Greek says "cubits" at 42:17 and in the second half of 42:20, and the Mishnah says the Temple Mount of the Second Temple measured 500 cubits by 500 (Middot 2:1). The Plain follows the Masoretic Text and offers the other in the variant.

a: to separate the holy from the ordinary
t: The purpose of the whole plan
p: The wall exists to divide holy from ordinary, the priests' duty in Leviticus 10:10.
b: The Hebrew lehavdil, "to separate", is the word of Leviticus 10:10, where the priests are to "distinguish" the holy from the ordinary, and 22:26 of this book accused the priests of not doing so. That charge is answered in 44:23: the priests are to teach the people the difference. The wall encloses the whole 500-cubit square, on all four sides, and it lets Ezekiel's Temple do what the old Temple did not: keep out what is not holy (43:8).

t: The east gate: the way out becomes the way in
p: The glory left the old Temple by the east (10:19; 11:23). It comes back by the same gate.
b: In 10:19 the glory of the God of Israel stood "at the entrance of the east gate", and in 11:23 it went up from the city and stood on the mountain to the east, the one we call the Mount of Olives. Now it returns from that direction. Zechariah 14:4 also puts the LORD on the Mount of Olives, east of Jerusalem. The rabbis counted ten journeys of the Shekhinah, the divine presence, as it moved from the Temple up to heaven (Rosh Hashanah 31a). In Christian use, Jesus entered Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives (Matthew 21:1-11), and Acts 1:9-12 puts his ascension there.

a: the glory of the God of Israel
t: The glory returns
p: The book's central image comes back: the same glory Ezekiel saw at the Kebar canal and watched leave.
b: The glory of the LORD appeared at the Kebar canal (1:28; 3:23), was in the old Temple (8:4), filled it with cloud (10:4), and left it in stages (9:3; 10:18-19; 11:22-23). Now it returns, with a noise like many waters, as in 1:24 (compare Revelation 1:15). The glory is not an abstraction; it is the visible presence of the LORD, and "the earth lit up" with it (compare Isaiah 60:1-2). This is the climax of the book. When the glory fills the house (43:5) the story of Exodus 40:34-35 and 1 Kings 8:10-11 repeats.

a: These visions were like the one I had seen by the Kebar canal.
t: Three visions that match
p: The prophet ties the new vision to two earlier ones: the call at the canal and the vision of the city's end.
b: Ezekiel names the two earlier visions that the sight resembles. One is "when I came to destroy the city" (chapters 8-11; the Hebrew has "I", the prophet announcing the destruction, as in Jeremiah 1:10 and Ezekiel 9:1-11). The other is the call by the Kebar canal (1:1-3:15). Both ended with the glory moving away; now the movement is reversed. The Greek reads "to anoint the city" and "the vision of the chariot" (see the variants). The Plain follows the Hebrew.

t: The same "spirit" that lifts him in 3:12 and 11:1
p: Ezekiel is carried by a spirit (ruach) several times. The Hebrew word also means wind and breath.
b: The Hebrew ruach is "spirit", "wind" or "breath". In Ezekiel a "spirit" lifts and carries the prophet (3:12, 14; 8:3; 11:1, 24; 37:1; 43:5), enters him and sets him on his feet (2:2; 3:24). The Plain uses "a spirit" here, as in 3:12, because the Hebrew has no "the". The bigger wordplay on ruach in chapter 37 is explained at 37:1.

a: the glory of the LORD filled the house
t: The glory fills the house: how it has been read
p: Jews, Christians and critical scholars read the return of the glory in different ways.
b: Jewish tradition remembers that the Second Temple lacked the glory: the Talmud lists five things missing from it, among them the Shekhinah (Yoma 21b). In that tradition the full return of the glory still lay ahead. Christian readers see it fulfilled in Jesus, in whom the Word "tabernacled" and in whose body is the Temple (John 1:14; 2:19-21), or in the church as the Temple (1 Corinthians 3:16; Ephesians 2:21-22). Revelation 21:22-23 has no temple, because the glory of God is the city's light. Critical scholars see this as the book's answer to the exile: the LORD, who had left, will return to a purified place.

t: The LORD's throne and footstool
p: The ark was called the LORD's footstool. Now the LORD says the whole house is his throne.
b: In the old Temple the ark was the LORD's footstool (1 Chronicles 28:2; Psalm 99:5; 132:7), and the cherubim above it were his throne (1 Samuel 4:4). Jeremiah 3:16-17 said that when the ark was no longer remembered, Jerusalem itself would be called the LORD's throne. Ezekiel speaks first: the place is the place of the LORD's own throne and the soles of his feet, and he will "live" there. Isaiah 66:1 says that heaven is his throne and earth is his footstool. Chapter 1 had the throne on the dome above the living creatures (1:26).

t: "The corpses of their kings": four readings
p: The meaning of this phrase, and of "high places", is not settled.
b: The Hebrew pigre malkehem bamotam can be read several ways. (1) Royal tombs: the kings were buried near the Temple (2 Kings 21:18, 26, where Manasseh and Amon were buried in the garden of their house), so that their graves defiled the holy place. (2) A cult of dead kings: offerings to the dead. (3) Idols: "corpses" as a scornful word for the idols, as in Leviticus 26:30 (pigre gillulim), with "kings" as "Molech" (melek; see Leviticus 18:21). (4) The last word, bamotam, may be "their high places" or "at their death". The Greek has "the killings of their leaders in their midst". The Plain follows the Hebrew and the "high places" reading.

t: The palace next to the Temple
p: In the old Jerusalem the king's house shared a wall with the Temple.
b: Solomon built his own palace and the house of the Forest of Lebanon next to the Temple in the same group of courts (1 Kings 7:1-12). The king had his own entrance to the Temple (2 Kings 16:18), and kings put things in the Temple that the LORD hated (2 Kings 21:4-7; 23:11-12). The charge in 43:8 is that threshold touched threshold. Ezekiel's answer is the wall of 42:20 and the rule that the leader may enter only the gate's porch (44:3; 46:2). See also 45:7-8.

a: describe the house to the house of Israel
t: Why show the Temple to people who must be ashamed?
p: The plan is to be shown so that the exiles feel shame. Readers have read the verse several ways.
b: The reading of the Plain is that the Temple plan itself shames the exiles, because it shows what the holy place ought to have been. In the Greek as printed in Swete, the text reads "they will stop sinning" and "they will receive their punishment" and has no "if" in 43:11. Some readers take the "if" as a condition: the plan will be given only to the repentant. Others take the shame as part of the vision's work. The plan is also meant to be written down (43:11), so that it can be kept as a pattern by later readers. See the settings for the chapter.

a: its arrangement, its exits and its entrances
t: The Hebrew list of plans and rules
p: The verse piles up words for design, shape and law, in a style that may reflect a text built up in stages.
b: The verse names the house's "design" (tsurah), "arrangement" (tekhunah), exits and entrances, "forms" (tsurot), "rules" (chuqqot) and "laws" (torot). It repeats "all its forms" and has Ketiv and Qere differences. The Greek is much shorter. The repetition has led some scholars to suspect added words. This verse treats the Temple's plan as "torah", a teaching to be kept; 43:12 ("the law of the house") and 44:5 do the same.

a: every bit of land around it is most holy
t: The whole mountaintop is "most holy"
p: In the Torah only the innermost room is "most holy". Here the whole area is.
b: In the law of Moses the "most holy place" is the room behind the veil (Exodus 26:33-34). Ezekiel widens it: all the ground on top of the mountain, the 500-cubit square of 42:20, is most holy. This is a change in how holiness is spread. In 44:9 and 45:1-4 the sacred area is also graded into zones. This is the "law of the house" (torat habbayit), the one law of the new Temple: holiness covers the place.

t: The Greek calls the ledge hilasterion
p: The Greek names the altar ledge with the word that renders the ark's cover in Exodus 25 and appears in Hebrews 9:5 and Romans 3:25.
b: The Hebrew 'azarah ("ledge") is rendered in the Greek of 43:14, 17 and 20 by hilasterion. This is the word the Greek of Exodus 25:17-22 uses for the cover of the ark, the mercy seat. The New Testament has it twice: Hebrews 9:5 ("the cherubim of glory, spreading their shadow over the atonement lid", where the lid is the hilasterion) and Romans 3:25, where God puts Christ forward as a hilasterion (see the topic on atonement for the translation debate). The shared word shows that the Greek translator heard "ledge" as a place of atonement, since blood is put on its corners in 43:20. It does not show that Paul or the writer of Hebrews had Ezekiel's altar in mind, and the Hebrew of Ezekiel does not call the ledge a mercy seat. The Plain follows the Hebrew.

t: The altar hearth: har'el or ari'el
p: Two spellings of a strange word: "mountain of God" or "lion of God". It is the top of the altar, where the fire burns.
b: The Hebrew text writes har'el, "mountain of God", in the first place (the Ketiv) and reads ari'el (the Qere); in 43:16 it reads ari'el. Isaiah 29:1-2 calls Jerusalem "Ariel" and plays on the word. The Mesha stele of Moab (line 12) has the same word, 'r'l, among the things its king dragged off, though what it names is uncertain. A link to Akkadian arallû, "mountain of the gods", has been proposed, and would make the stepped altar a model mountain. The Plain says "hearth" and keeps the Hebrew in a gloss.

t: The horns of the altar
p: The corners of the altar were where blood was put, and where a person in danger could grab hold.
b: The altar of the Tabernacle had horns on its four corners (Exodus 27:2), and the priest put the sin offering's blood on them (Leviticus 4:7, 18, 25, 30). A person could hold the horns for safety (1 Kings 1:50-51; 2:28). The MT says "four horns"; the Greek says the horns rise "a cubit" above the hearth (see the variants). The blood on the horns is the first step in 43:20.

a: The steps up to it face east.
t: Steps to the altar, against Exodus 20:26?
p: Ezekiel's altar has steps. The law of Moses said not to climb to the altar by steps.
b: Exodus 20:26 says: do not go up to my altar by steps, so your nakedness is not uncovered. Ezekiel's altar has steps. Exodus 28:42 gives the priests linen undergarments for this reason, and the Mishnah describes the Second Temple's altar as reached by a ramp on the south (Middot 3:3). Shabbat 13b tells how the sages nearly shelved the book because Ezekiel's words seemed to contradict the Torah. Readers harmonize it by pointing to the priests' undergarments, or accept that Ezekiel's rules differ from Moses's.
r: Exodus 20:26; Exodus 28:42; Mishnah Middot 3:1-3; Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 13b

t: The first rules given by the LORD in the vision
p: After the tour, the LORD himself speaks: here are the rules for the day the altar is made.
b: Here the guide passes on a word of the Lord GOD: rules (chuqqot) for the day the altar is made. They resemble Moses's rules in Exodus 29:35-37 (seven days, a sin offering to cleanse the altar) and Leviticus 8:14-17 (the bull, the blood on the horns). The differences are in the animals: Ezekiel uses a bull on the first day, a goat on days 2-7 (43:22, 25), and adds a bull and a ram for burnt offerings (43:23-25). Exodus 29:36 has a bull each day. The Greek has "two kids" for the goat. The Plain says "flawless" for tamim in the animals of 43:22-25, as the site does in Leviticus.

a: the Levite priests who are of the offspring of Zadok
t: Zadok again, and the "you"
p: The sin-offering bull is handed to the Zadokite priests. The "you" is Ezekiel, who stands where Moses stood.
b: These are the priests of 40:46 and 44:15: Zadok's family, a sub-group of the Levites. The Plain says "Levite priests" (the term of Deuteronomy 17:9, 18) and gives the family name. The command "you are to give" is addressed to Ezekiel, who is told to do what Moses did when the Tabernacle was opened (Leviticus 8). Ezekiel was himself a priest (1:3).

t: Cleansing the altar
p: The sin offering here cleans the altar, not a person. A leading scholar argues this is what it does everywhere.
b: The Hebrew verb chitte' is "to remove sin", from the same root as chatta't, the "sin offering". Here the blood is put on the altar, not on a person: the altar must be cleansed before it is used (compare Leviticus 8:15; Exodus 29:36-37). Jacob Milgrom argued that the chatta't in the law always cleans the sanctuary of the impurity that the people's sin brings in, and the site's term note keeps "sin offering" with his "purification offering" view in mind. Ezekiel 45:18-20 repeats the idea for the Temple itself.

t: Burning the bull outside
p: The sin offering's body is burned outside, as in Leviticus 4:12 and 16:27. Hebrews 13:11-13 uses that fact.
b: The body of a sin offering is burned outside the camp (Leviticus 4:12, 21; 16:27). In Ezekiel the burning is in the "appointed place" (mifqad) of the house, outside the sanctuary. Nehemiah 3:31 names a "Miphkad Gate" in Jerusalem's wall. Hebrews 13:11-13 refers to the same practice: the bodies are burned outside the camp, and Jesus suffered outside the gate.

t: Salt on the offerings
p: Leviticus 2:13 requires salt on every offering. Ezekiel is the one who mentions it on animals.
b: Leviticus 2:13 says that every grain offering must have salt, the salt of God's covenant, and that salt must go with all offerings. Ezekiel is the one who shows it on animal offerings (see also Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5). The salt keeps the offering from rotting and stands for what lasts, the covenant.

t: "Fill its hand": installing the altar
p: The Hebrew idiom is the one for ordaining a priest. Here it is used of the altar, in the Greek of the priests.
b: The Hebrew idiom mille' yad, "fill the hand", means to install or ordain, and is used of priests (Exodus 29:9, 33; Leviticus 8:33). The written text (Ketiv) has "its hand" and the reading tradition (Qere) "its hands"; the Plain gives the sense. The Greek has "they will fill their hands", which puts the priests, not the altar, in the role of those installed (see the variant). The result is the same: by the end of seven days the altar and its priests are ready to serve.

t: "I will accept you": a promise from chapter 20
p: The vision ends on the LORD's promise. The same word was used in chapter 20 for the new beginning.
b: The verb ratsah, "accept", is the one used in 20:40-41: on the holy mountain the whole house of Israel will serve the LORD, and he will accept them and their offerings. The ending of 43 matches it. The "eighth day" is the day after the seven of the altar's dedication (compare Leviticus 9:1, where Aaron begins his work on the eighth day). Offerings on the new altar are not just rules; they are the place where the LORD's acceptance is received.
